a: [Love the Lord all your life,
t: A verse found only in the longer text
p: Vaticanus has no line here. The longer Greek and the Latin have it; both lines of the verse go together.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete's notes record no line in Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus either; Hebrew manuscript A (Kahana) also lacks it
readings.en: (no line)

readings.w: Minuscules 106, 248 and 253, in J. H. A. Hart's edition of 248 (1909); Latin Vulgate 13:18 "Omni vita tua dilige Deum, et invoca illum in salute tua"; KJV
readings.orig: πάσῃ ζωῇ ἀγάπα τὸν κύριον καὶ ἐπικαλοῦ αὐτὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν σου
readings.en: all your life love the Lord and call on him for your salvation
readings.plain: [Love the Lord all your life,

why: Every verse number needs a line, so the Plain gives this one in square brackets, translated from Hart's text of minuscule 248 and the Vulgate, which agree. The brackets show it is not in Codex Vaticanus, the base text. Hart notes that the line looks like a reworking of the next verse's "every living thing loves"; it is a pious addition of the longer text, not part of the grandson's translation.
b: Hart's commentary gives the longer reading as part of an addition at the end of 13:13: "hearing these things in your sleep, wake up; all your life love the Lord..." (minuscules 106, 248, 253). The Latin has the same two lines as its 13:17-18.

a: in the mouth of the ungodly
t: Godly or ungodly?
p: Vaticanus reads "godly"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "ungodly," as the KJV does. The Plain departs from Vaticanus here.

readings.plain: in the mouth of the insolent

why: This is one of the few places where the Plain leaves Swete's Vaticanus. "Godly" makes poor sense: the couplet sets wealth without sin against poverty as the arrogant see it, and the Hebrew "insolent" supports Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus. A single letter (eusebous / asebous) separates the two Greek words, an easy slip for a copyist.

a: it happens when he forgets himself
t: By forgetting, or unwillingly?
p: Vaticanus says he does good "in forgetfulness"; minuscule 248, followed by the KJV, says "unwillingly."

a: bring the Lord the offerings he deserves
t: Offerings to the Lord, or "make yourself fat"?
p: The Greek speaks of offerings to the Lord; the Hebrew tells the student to enjoy his means. The two may come from one Hebrew word.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ προσφορὰς Κυρίῳ ἀξίως πρόσαγε
readings.en: and bring offerings to the Lord worthily
readings.plain: bring the Lord the offerings he deserves

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863, folio A VI recto), in Kahana's edition (1912)
readings.orig: וּלְאֵל יָדְךָ הִדָּשֵׁן
readings.en: and as far as your hand can, make yourself fat (enjoy plenty)
readings.plain: as far as your hand can reach, enjoy plenty

why: The Plain translates the Greek. Hart (1909) suggests why the two differ: the Hebrew idiom le'el yadkha, "as your hand is able," begins with the letters of le'el, "to God," and the Greek took it that way, then supplied offerings. The Hebrew fits the context (14:11-16 is about enjoying one's goods), but the Greek is the text the churches received.
b: Offerings to God do fit Ben Sira's thought elsewhere (7:31; 35:10-12), so the Greek is not out of place even if it arose from a misreading.

readings.plain: pamper yourself

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus, which the Hebrew "pamper yourself" supports. Greek apataō usually means "deceive," but with "your soul" it means to divert or cheer yourself. Later copyists and translators found that worldly and changed it to "sanctify" or "justify."

p: The Greek says the Lord will prosper praise; the Hebrew says the one who masters wisdom will teach it.

a: for what he hates you are not to do
t: "You are not to do" or "he did not do"?
p: The Greek gives a command to the reader; the Hebrew says God himself did not do (or make) what he hates.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: ἃ γὰρ ἐμίσησεν, οὐ ποιήσεις

readings.plain: for what he hates you are not to do

readings.en: for what he hates he did not do (or: make)
readings.plain: for what he hates he did not do

why: The Plain translates the Greek, the base text. Many modern translations follow the Hebrew here, which fits the argument better: God cannot be the cause of sin, because he does not do what he hates. The Hebrew of the first line also differs: "My transgression is from God." The Greek has "because of the Lord I fell away."

a: He himself sent me off course
t: "He led me astray" or "He made me so"?
p: Several later Greek copies read "he formed me" instead of "he led me astray," turning the excuse into "God made me this way."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: Αὐτός με ἐπλάνησεν
readings.en: he himself led me astray
readings.plain: He himself sent me off course

readings.orig: Αὐτός με ἔπλασεν
readings.en: he himself formed me
readings.plain: He himself made me this way

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863, folio A VI recto), in Kahana's edition (1912)
readings.orig: הוּא הִתְקִילָנִי
readings.en: he himself made me stumble
readings.plain: He himself made me stumble

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. "Formed me" (eplasen for eplanēsen) is an easy copying change, but it gives the excuse a sharper edge: if God shaped me with this nature, my sin is his doing. 15:14 answers exactly that: he made the human being free to choose.

a: left him in the hand of his own choice
t: A doubled line in the Hebrew: "his robber"
p: The Hebrew has two lines where the Greek has one: God put man "in the hand of his robber" and "of his yetser."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: καὶ ἀφῆκεν αὐτὸν ἐν χειρὶ διαβουλίου αὐτοῦ

readings.plain: left him in the hand of his own choice

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863, folio A VI recto), in Kahana's edition (1912)
readings.orig: וַיְשִׁיתֵהוּ בְּיַד חוֹתְפוֹ, וַיִּתְּנֵהוּ בְּיַד יִצְרוֹ

Hart (1909) explains the Hebrew "robber" (chotfo, one who seizes) as an addition that interprets the yetser as the evil inclination that snatches a person away; the Greek and the Latin know only one line, and the extra line clashes with the argument that people are free.

a: keeping faith is for you to choose
t: A line only in the Hebrew: "If you trust in him, you will live"
p: The Hebrew adds a third line close to Habakkuk 2:4.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ πίστιν ποίησαι εὐδοκίας

readings.plain: keeping faith is for you to choose

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863, folio A VI recto), in Kahana's edition (1912)
readings.orig: וְתָבִינָה לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ אִם תַּאֲמִין בּוֹ גַּם אַתָּה, תִּחְיֶה

readings.plain: understanding is doing his will. / If you trust in him, you too will live

why: The Plain translates the Greek. Hart (1909) suggests that the Greek "faith" (pistis) comes from a Hebrew word for faithfulness read where manuscript A has "understanding," and that the Hebrew third line ("if you trust in him, you too will live") grew from the same variant, recalling Habakkuk 2:4, "the righteous will live by his faithfulness." The Latin adds "he added his commandments and precepts" before this verse, which Luther quotes in his reply to Erasmus.
